title: Why Daisy Edgar-Jones Listened to Dolly Parton to Prep for ‘Sense and Sensibility’
description:

	She knows how to please hardcore fans while offering a fresh take on
body:
Daisy Edgar-Jones is no stranger to starring in a book-to-screen adaptation.

	She knows how to please hardcore fans while offering a fresh take on the material. (See the success of “Normal People” and “Where the Crawdads Are” or the upcoming “Tomorrow and Tomorrow and Tomorrow” as proof.) That said, starring in a Jane Austen adaptation is a different beast altogether — but Edgar-Jones has been an Austen admirer from an early age.
	

	“My mum gave me all the books when I was at a very formative age,” Edgar-Jones told Variety at the Los Angeles premiere of “Sense and Sensibility,” in which she stars as Elinor Dashwood. “It’s a rite of passage to read them all when you’re a teenager, and you’re finding yourself and falling in love for the first time and experience that personal growth. So, yeah, I read them in one fell swoop.”


	Even then, Edgar-Jones connected with the eldest Dashwood daughter, known for her good sense — certainly more so than her passionate sister Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles).

	“I really enjoy playing characters that have a deep well inside that maybe other people overlook, and finding ways in which to express that,” Edgar-Jones explained. “She’s somebody that has such a strength and this deep well of emotion that she’s learned to button up. And I love the journey she goes on where she becomes more comfortable with embracing that wilder side of herself. I was just so excited to sink my teeth into playing her.

	To prepare for her roles, Edgar-Jones listens to songs that get her into the character’s headspace. To promote the film release, Edgar-Jones shared her “Sense and Sensibility” playlist, which ranges from legends like Billie Holiday, Minnie Riperton and Dolly Parton to contemporary artists like Alice Pheobe Lou, Julia Jacklin and Jessica Pratt.
	


	Why include Parton’s “Here You Come Again?” Well, Edgar-Jones used to belt that track in the car on the way home from school.

	“It just epitomizes what it is to like love somebody — that heartbreak and slight female rage inside that you just want to let out. I really could imagine, if Eleanor lived in a time with Dolly Parton, she’d be belting that around her bedroom in Barton [Cottage].”



	

					Esmé Creed-Miles, Caitríona Balfe and Daisy Edgar-Jones at the “Sense & Sensibility” Los Angeles premiere.
									Michael Buckner
	



	At the Oct. 7 premiere, held at the United Theatre in Downtown L.A., Edgar-Jones was joined by her film family, including Caitríona Balfe, who plays their mother, Mrs. Dashwood, and Creed-Miles, who was named one of Variety’s 10 Actors to Watch earlier that day.

	“It’s a bit scary,” Creed-Miles said about having so many eyes drawn to her work. “I just really care about filmmakers, and Georgia [Oakley] is a really special one. I was a big fan of “Blue Jean,” so going into this, I wasn’t thinking about that side of it. I’ve never experienced anything on this level of like support, and that’s really special.”

	Creed-Miles also reflected on the amplified sisterhood narrative in the film, as screenwriter Diana Reid (also a Variety 10 to Watch honoree) adapted the script to center more on the relationship between Elinor and Marianne.

	“I’m family with these women: Georgia, Diana, Daisy is one of my absolute best friends, everyone,” Creed-Miles said. “Amazing women were involved in the making of this film. There was something cathartic and really rewarding about having a family making something — and a family of sisters, as well.”



	

					“Sense and Sensibility” stars Herbert Nordrum, Stacy Martin, Frank Dillane, Caitriona Balfe, Esmé Creed-Miles and Daisy Edgar-Jones at the L.A. premiere after-party.
									Michael Buckner

schema.headline: Why Daisy Edgar-Jones Listened to Dolly Parton to Prep for ‘Sense and Sensibility’

title: Bob Buziak, Former President of RCA Records and Sony’s Tristar Music Group, Dies at 83
description: Bob Buziak, former president of both RCA Records and Sony’s TriStar Music Group, died on October 19, a rep confirms to Variety. No cause of death w
body:
Bob Buziak, former president of both RCA Records and Sony’s TriStar Music Group, died on October 19, a rep confirms to Variety. No cause of death was announced; he was 83.

	Buziak was best known for reviving RCA’s fortunes in the 1980s with hit albums by Bruce Hornsby, Eurythmics and Love and Rockets, not to mention the blockbuster soundtracks to the “Dirty Dancing” films, which spawned a No. 1 single with Eric Carmen’s “Hungry Eyes” and an Oscar- and Grammy-winner with Bill Medley and Jennifer Warnes’ “(I’ve Had) The Time of My Life.”
	

	He left a job at the Ford Motor Company in 1968 to work in the music business, taking on distribution and promotion roles in Detroit and San Francisco before joining Capitol/EMI Records in Los Angeles. He held promotion and A&R roles at that label before joining Arista Records, where he thrived as head of West Coast operations and, later, managing director in the U.K. His performance at that label led directly to his being named president of RCA in 1986.


	While there, Buziak’s distribution deals with indie labels like Beggars Banquet (which brought Love and Rockets and others) and Jive helped expand and modernize the label’s roster.

	He left the label in 1990 to serve as president of Sony’s TriStar Music Group and later founded Chameleon Entertainment as a joint venture with Time Warner. In 1995, he launched Buziak & Company LLC, which consulted for telecom and cable companies, and played a key role in the sale of Paradigm Music Entertainment to Liberty Media.

	He was a board member of inVentures a U.K. investment group and initiated a merger with Redwood Partners a U.S. corporate search firm to create a multi-platform international consulting and venture group.

schema.headline: Bob Buziak, Former President of RCA Records and Sony’s Tristar Music Group, Dies at 83

title: Ann Hornaday, Longtime Washington Post Film Critic and Pulitzer Prize Finalist, Dies at 66
description: Ann Hornaday, the longtime film critic at The Washington Post, died Sunday at her home in Baltimore following a battle with glioblastoma, a form of
body:
Ann Hornaday, the longtime film critic at The Washington Post, died Sunday at her home in Baltimore following a battle with glioblastoma, a form of brain cancer. She was 66.

	Hornaday spent more than 20 years at the Post, joining in 2002 and leaving in 2025. Over the course of her time at the Post, she wrote hundreds of reviews, in-depth profiles and stories, including deep looks at films like “The Hurt Locker,” “Jaws” and “Oppenheimer.”
	

	“For many years, Post readers were blessed by Ann’s informed, insightful, warm, accessible, and totally unique voice,” said Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray in a statement published by the paper. “Reading her work was like talking with a close — if much more knowledgeable — friend.”


	Hornaday was a 2008 Pulitzer Prize finalist in criticism, submitting her review of “There Will Be Blood,” among other works, in her finalist package. She also authored “Talking Pictures,” a book about how to watch films, and before her death, a book about the filming of “All the President’s Men.”

	Before Hornaday became the influential critic she is remembered as, she worked as a freelance writer in New York, contributing to publications including The New York Times and Premiere magazine. Prior to that, she worked at Ms. Magazine for two years as Gloria Steinem’s personal assistant. She was the film critic for the Baltimore Sun and the Austin American-Statesman before joining the Post. 

	Ann Mills Hornaday was born March 9, 1960, in Iowa City. At birth, she was adopted by William R. Hornaday Jr. and his wife, Mary Mills. Hornaday grew up in Des Moines and attended Smith College, graduating in 1982 with a major in government. 
	

	While a film critic, she was also a parishioner and Sunday school teacher in Baltimore.

	She is survived by her husband of 26 years, Dennis Greenia; their daughter, Victoria Greenia; a stepdaughter, Leila Greenia; and a brother, William Hornaday III.

schema.headline: Ann Hornaday, Longtime Washington Post Film Critic and Pulitzer Prize Finalist, Dies at 66

title: ‘Star Wars’ Comes to 2027 Super Bowl With Animated ‘Alterna-Cast’ for Disney Channel, XD, Disney+
description: Add C-3PO to the list of popular Disney personalities who will be guiding football fans through sundry telecasts of ESPN‘s coverage of Super Bowl L
body:
Add C-3PO to the list of popular Disney personalities who will be guiding football fans through sundry telecasts of ESPN‘s coverage of Super Bowl LXI in 2027.

	The golden droid, a mainstay of Disney’s “Star Wars” movies from Lucasfilm, will play a significant role in a real-time, animated telecast of the Big Game that will be set in the “universe” of the movie franchise and air across Disney+, Disney Channel, Disney XD and the ESPN App on Sunday, February 14. Actor Anthony Daniels, who originally played the character, will take part in the spectacle. Meanwhile, five other productions of the 2027 Super Bowl are slated for ESPN, ABC, ESPN2 and ESPNU, among other Disney media properties.
	

	The animated telecast, dubbed “Star Wars Funday Football,” will recreate every play of Super Bowl LXI as it happens, but transform players on the field into animated avatars. Characters from “Star Wars” will sub in at key moments and surprise nods to the films will appear throughout the match. Disney is able to transform live gameplay into animation by combining player tracking data from the NFL’s Next Gen Stats and Sony’s Hawk-Eye Innovations optical tracking. 


	The company said it expects to unveil more details, such as visual settings, commentators and characters, in weeks to come.

	Disney continues to broaden the viewing options for its airing of Super Bowl LXI, the first gridiron classic the company has had under its purview in about two decades. Earlier this month, Disney tapped outspoken host Pat McAfee to anchor “Field Pass,” a commentary-driven option, that will play alongside a traditional broadcast of the Big Game on ABC and ESPN, and a Super Bowl version of the popular “ManningCast” featuring Peyton and Eli Manning, on ESPN2. The company will offer a statistics-focused Super Bowl telecast, “Playbook,” which will be led by a team to be announced later, and air on NFL Network, as well as a Spanish-language telecast on ESPN Deportes.
	

	A Super Bowl “mega cast” has been in consideration at the company since 2021, when Disney struck a new rights deal with the NFL that keeps “Monday Night Football” on the air at ESPN through 2033. Since that time, the league and the company have become even closer, with the league taking a 10% stake in ESPN as part of a deal that put NFL Network and NFL RedZone under the ESPN umbrella.

	Other companies have tried to interest TV’s smallest viewers in the biggest annual event the medium has to offer. The media conglomerate previously known as Paramount aired a kids’ version of the Super Bowl on Nickelodeon in 2024. Disney, meanwhile, has at various moments over the years tapped animated figures ranging from the “Toy Story” crew to “Big City Green” characters to Marvel superheroes to create bespoke NFL, NHL and NBA games for the wee set. 

	Five days after the company airs its growing array of Super Bowl telecasts, Lucasfilm will celebrate 50 years of the “Star Wars” franchise by putting a restored version of the original 1977 movie in theaters, starting Friday, February 19.

schema.headline: ‘Star Wars’ Comes to 2027 Super Bowl With Animated ‘Alterna-Cast’ for Disney Channel, XD, Disney+

title: Rita Wilson Says She’s Returning for Lena Dunham’s ‘Girls’ Revival: ‘I Would Do Anything for Her’
description: Evie Michaels is back! Rita Wilson is teasing plans to reprise her “Girls” role as Marnie Michael’s eccentric mother in Lena Dunham’s much-anticipa
body:
Evie Michaels is back! Rita Wilson is teasing plans to reprise her “Girls” role as Marnie Michael’s eccentric mother in Lena Dunham’s much-anticipated revival.

	When asked by People if she’ll be returning for the new iteration of the hit show, Wilson told the publication, “That is what I’m hearing, so I don’t think Lena would be lying about that.” The actress went on to say that she is “so excited” about the series return, Wilson first joined the show during Season 2 and made guest appearances throughout the show’s run. 
	

	“Oh my gosh, yes. I mean, Lena is one of the most talented people I’ve ever worked with. I would do anything for her,” she continued. “I would bend over backward. And then I love Allison Williams who, you know, I was lucky enough to play her mom.” She added: “I know Lena’s gotta be cooking up something very good.”


	Earlier this month, it was announced that HBO had greenlit a revival of “Girls,” the dramedy created by Dunham. The series will return for a limited, five-episode run with production beginning in 2027 — a decade after the Season 6 finale.

	With Dunham as creator, showrunner and star, the original series ran from 2012 to 2017 and followed a group of friends through the misery and dysfunction of their 20s in New York City. All four core cast members are returning for the revival: Dunham as Hannah Horvath, Allison Williams as Marnie Michaels, Jemima Kirke as Jessa Johansson and Zosia Mamet as Shoshanna Shapiro. Additionally, Andrew Rannells reprises the role of Elijah Krantz.

	Wilson first joined the show during Season 2 and made guest appearances throughout the show’s run. 
	

	Judd Apatow returns as executive producer on behalf of Apatow Productions alongside Dunham, Ilene S. Landress and Michael P. Cohen of Dunham’s Good Thing Going banner. Williams, Kirke, Mamet and Rannells serve as co-executive producers.

schema.headline: Rita Wilson Says She’s Returning for Lena Dunham’s ‘Girls’ Revival: ‘I Would Do Anything for Her’

title: Why ‘Office Space’ Actor Richard Riehle Was the Quintessential Actor’s Actor (Guest Column)
description: The first time I met Richard Riehle, I was making one of the first things I’d ever made. It was a Funny or Die video, and my friend Tanner Thomason
body:
The first time I met Richard Riehle, I was making one of the first things I’d ever made. It was a Funny or Die video, and my friend Tanner Thomason and I were trying to figure out how to get an actual actor to be in it. Someone suggested Richard. “Just offer it to him. I bet he’ll be down.” So we wrote him a nice letter, offered him the enormous sum of $250, and a week later we were working with a legend.

	I remember arriving on set that morning and finding Richard already there, sitting by himself, reading the newspaper and drinking a root beer. He’d beaten the crew there. He didn’t need anything, didn’t seem particularly concerned that he was an actor with hundreds of credits doing a little internet video for two guys who had never really made anything before. He was just happy to be there.
	

	That was about 13 years ago. I spent a lot of the next 13 years trying to find reasons to work with him again. If I wrote something with a part Richard could play, I offered it to him. Sometimes I probably wrote the part because I wanted an excuse to hear his stories. We ended up acting in several other projects together, too, and over the years we became friends.


	He was also, without question, one of the best actors I’ve ever worked with. I know that might sound like the sort of thing people say when someone dies, but I mean it. Richard was astonishingly good. He could make a line funny just by deciding not to make it funny. He could steal a scene without seeming to do much of anything. And every once in a while he’d remind you that underneath the familiar face and the wonderful mustache was an actor with a range most people never got to see.
	

	Years ago, we were doing a table read for a movie called “Fear, Inc.” We’d cast Richard as the funny neighbor. The actor who was supposed to read the villain couldn’t make it that night, so Richard offered to fill in. No big deal. Just reading a few extra lines. Then he started doing the role, which he had literally worked on at home. He knew the lines of a role he wasn’t even going to play for the table read. The sweet, funny neighbor we’d all been laughing at was suddenly terrifying. I remember looking around the room and seeing jaws drop. People were genuinely stunned. It was like we’d all forgotten, for a moment, who we were sitting across from.

	Richard had more than 400 acting credits, which is an almost ridiculous number until you understand the man. More than anything, he just loved being on set. Student films, tiny independent movies, major blockbusters, network sitcoms. I honestly don’t think he cared all that much about the difference. If he could hang out on set instead of in his trailer, that’s where you’d find him. And if you worked with him once, you had a friend. Invite him to a screening a year later, some random improv show, or a backyard barbecue, and if he was free, he’d show up.

	A couple of years ago, we were in Dallas shooting a movie called Tonic. One night over beers, Richard told me how excited he was to have been asked to reunite with his old “Office Space” pal, Stephen Root, on an episode of “Barry.” We got to talking about his career, and he said something I’ve thought about a lot since. Richard suspected that taking so many small independent projects over the years had probably hurt his chances of getting certain television or studio jobs. Maybe people saw the sheer volume of credits and made assumptions. Maybe he’d have been better off being more selective. But he wasn’t going to change anything.

	He wanted to act. As much as he could, for as long as he could. If saying yes to some tiny movie meant missing out on a bigger one, well, that was fine with him. He’d rather spend his Tuesday on a set somewhere, even a tiny set, than sit around waiting for a more prestigious phone call. I loved that about him. I think a lot of us could learn something from it.

	Richard lived in the same Los Feliz spot for years. He liked being able to walk around Hillhurst and Vermont, to get out and be part of the neighborhood. He drove a Honda Civic that was something like 25 years old. Why get a new car? This one worked. It got him to set and back. That was Richard.
	

	And he had that mustache. I’m actually wearing a mustache today partially because of Richard Riehle. Six years ago, I grew one for a movie we made together called “Faith Based.” I wasn’t sure I was going to keep it. Richard told me I should. He said growing his own mustache was one of the best decisions he’d ever made. It fit his face, he explained, and gave him something distinctive. Coming from a man whose mustache belongs in the same conversation as Sam Elliott’s and Burt Reynolds’, I took that advice pretty seriously. I haven’t shaved it since. I suppose that’s a pretty small thing to carry forward from a friendship, but I like knowing that a little piece of Richard will be looking back at me in the mirror every morning.

	When I think about Richard now, I don’t really think about his filmography, impressive as it is. I think about that first morning. The newspaper and the root beer. A man who’d already been in more movies than I could count, sitting patiently on the set of a $250 internet video in Canoga Park, ready to give it everything he had for a comedy sketch.

	He gave that little project just as much as he would have given a studio movie. I don’t think it ever occurred to him to do otherwise. Richard just loved being an actor.

	Luke Barnett is an actor, writer, and filmmaker whose credits include AMC’s “Dark Winds,” Apple TV+’s “For All Mankind” and Peacock’s “The Burbs.” His recent filmmaking work includes the viral short “The Crossing Over Express,” currently being developed as a feature, and the Fangoria-produced “Goodbye, Monster,” which just premiered at Fantastic Fest. He has also worked on nearly a dozen projects with the late Richard Riehle, though not nearly enough.

schema.headline: Why ‘Office Space’ Actor Richard Riehle Was the Quintessential Actor’s Actor (Guest Column)

title: Role Model Shouts Out Jake Shane and Renee Rapp, Channels Chuck Timely on Final North American Tour Date: Concert Report
description: Without stretching the metaphor too far, Chuck Timely’s hourglass was closer to running out than he might have thought: While the second of two Lo
body:
Without stretching the metaphor too far, Chuck Timely’s hourglass was closer to running out than he might have thought: While the second of two Los Angeles dates of Role Model’s “Chuck on Tour” jaunt in support of his third studio album — titled (naturally enough) “Chuck Timely & the Hourglass” — was scheduled to be the second-to-last North American show, it actually was the last, as he canceled the next night’s final stop in Berkeley due to illness.
	

	However, there was no sign of illness at the Greek Theatre on Friday night, as Role Model took the stage in his latest persona, the time-traveler Chuck Timely. (He was the Saint Laurent Cowboy for his 2024 album “Kansas Anymore.”) He has described his new character as someone who’s “been around through all the eras and seems to grab little pieces from each along the way. He’s been around forever.”

	The show started on a slightly awkward note, as Role Model made a grand entrance to a pre-recorded “Chuck’s Mantra,” emerging from the darkness for “High Hopes 3000.” But when the track dropped out for a few moments, a confused silence overtook the 6,000-strong audience. And when the track finally resumed, the lyrics were nearly drowned out by the eruption of cheers as Pillsbury’s silhouette was illuminated by golden lights.


	With that, the energy kicked in. “I don’t say this every night, and I didn’t say it last night,” he shouted, “but you can tell when a show is going to be fucking lit one song in — and tonight’s going to be a fun night!”

	Pillsbury maintained the energy throughout his 90-minute set, alternating between singing and playing acoustic and electric guitars, with the energy only slowing down for lower-key songs like “The Longest Goodbye” and “Good Thing,” the latter of which inspired hundreds of fans to wave their phone flashlights.
	

	The stage set was kept simple, with comical placements cards for each of the bandmembers, including “Bass God,” “Piano Man” and, of course, “Chuck,” while a marker at the back of the stage read, “Stand here for the drama.”

	Though he didn’t stand in the designated spot, Pillsbury reminded the audience of the drama surrounding his track “Love I You,” which features his now-ex Dakota Johnson. Rather than use Johnson’s voice during the live performance, Pillsbury invites someone from the audience each night to recite the song’s popular back-and-forth.

	But the setlist dipped into Role Model’s pre-Chuck eras, including “Writing’s on the Wall,” “Slipfast,” “Old Recliners” and, of course, the evening’s most-anticipated song, “Sally, When the Wine Runs Out.”

	The night also had, as he put it, “some tea”: not only were Role Model’s parents in the house, but he also said that his friend, online personality Jake Shane, had attended Thursday night’s show because he knew singer Reneé Rapp would be at Friday’s.

	“He wanted all the fucking attention on him, so he decided to come last night because he knew Reneé would take all the attention from him,” Pillsbury told the crowd. “And that’s fucking true!”

	As the audience erupted in cheers and scanned the crowd for Rapp, Pillsbury said, “All right stop looking at her, look at me,” he laughed. “I got fucking dressed up for you.”

schema.headline: Role Model Shouts Out Jake Shane and Renee Rapp, Channels Chuck Timely on Final North American Tour Date: Concert Report

title: Why Netflix Fired Dan Lin (and the Truth About His Tension With Greta Gerwig Over ‘Narnia’)
description: “Everyone is collateral damage.”That’s how one top Netflix insider summarized another bloody Monday at the streamer, which saw Dan Lin ousted as the
body: “Everyone is collateral damage.”That’s how one top Netflix insider summarized another bloody Monday at the streamer, which saw Dan Lin ousted as the company’s head of film.Following last week’s 6% workforce reduction at Netflix – which claimed victims including chief content officer Bela Bajaria and Lin’s right-hand Doug Belgrad – consensus said it was a matter of time before co-CEO Ted Sarandos would show Lin the door.It took a day. On the heels of the Bajaria news on Thursday, Sarandos rang Lin on Friday to tell him he’d been dismissed, three sources told Variety. The exec kept his head up and pressed on through the weekend, appearing at Saturday’s Academy Gala (in the same room as Sarandos) and at a Sunday tastemaker screening to support the filmmakers of “La Bola Negra.” As has been summarized in many articles about the Netflix purge, creative leadership at the company is being overhauled amid poor stock performance and declining user engagement on the platform. Peter Rice, the veteran film and TV executive, will now preside over and shake up the platform’s content.Competing narratives are flying about why Lin was let go, but they arrive at the same conclusion: In the end, it wasn’t working. This, despite Lin meeting his mandates to curb spending and make movies that resonated with subscribers. In firing Lin and Bajaria and ushering in Rice, some say Sarandos was desperate to sell a story about growth to Wall Street (Netflix’s quarterly earnings report drops Tuesday). Others say Lin could not dance fast enough to find the balance between sticky streaming titles and theatrical release experiments (in fairness, he made it halfway through a five-year deal, barely enough time to get a casting announcement together by today’s standards). There are also some interesting leaks around tension he’s said to have with A-list filmmakers like Greta Gerwig and Ben Affleck, which we’ll get to.The Lin era at Netflix was framed around austerity, both by the town and in some ways by “The Lego Movie” producer himself. A June profile in the New York Times declared Lin was done “coddling” Hollywood, bragging he did not “fawn over stars or write blank checks.” The implication was that his predecessor Scott Stuber had overpaid for talent and too-ambitiously committed to a new Netflix movie release every week in 2022. Those efforts scaled back gradually until Stuber exited in mid-2024.Lin entered with a red pen and a machete, the lore goes, in hopes of emphasizing quality over quantity. Some find it convenient that Stuber’s legacy is still being kicked up, perhaps to provide cloud cover for decisions made by Lin and his former boss Bajaria. Amid the noise of the current Netflix layoffs, it’s important to remember that the prevailing logic at Netflix for a long, long time was “we don’t give a shit about theatrical,” said one colorful studio source. Releasing movies in theaters was never part of the Netflix business model. Stuber paid premiums to get filmmakers like Martin Scorsese, Alfonso Cuarón and Rian Johnson on the service. He also worked with fervor to make the theatrical exhibitors accept Netflix titles in any capacity. While they refused at the time, individuals familiar with Sarandos said Stuber laid the groundwork for the inevitable – that the only way to create value around movies is to put them in theaters first.Lin brought this logic to fruition in convincing Sarandos that family-driven IP should receive robust, exclusive theatrical windows before moving on to streaming, individuals with knowledge of Lin said. We’ll see the results next year when Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” and “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” come to cineplexes.Where Netflix once organized its internal film teams by the budget range of projects they worked on, Lin grouped his executives according to genre expertise. He also moved swiftly to program release windows left empty by Stuber’s exit (“Nonnas,” “Happy Gilmore 2,” “The Thursday Murder Club”). He spent one day of his work week with the Netflix animation team, where he installed Hannah Minghella as a leader. For the core slate, Lin is credited with wooing Alan Ritchson (“War Machine”), Matthew McConaughey and Ben Stiller for upcoming projects.In the weeks before his exit, reports said Lin clashed with filmmaker Affleck (director of the just-released “Animals”) over the use of his AI platform InterPositive. Perhaps more consequential was a rift with Gerwig this summer over the upcoming “Narnia.” The movie represents a $250 million theatrical-first gamble.Four sources with knowledge of the matter said that, indeed, Lin and Gerwig had a falling out during a Zoom call about the project earlier this year. On a virtual meeting populated by numerous Netflix executives, Lin is said to have been “dismissive” to the director in conversation about the progress of the film. Lin is known in town to be incredibly fair, but at times obtuse in his frankness. Word travelled fast around Netflix that the meeting had gone south, at which point sources said Bajaria called Gerwig’s producer Amy Pascal to smooth things over. Two sources also said that Gerwig’s new, all-powerful CAA agent Bryan Lourd went to Sarandos directly over the faux pas. Lin was subsequently disappeared from the film, all sources concurred, and Belgrad stepped in as the primary Netflix exec overseeing the project (until, of course, he was laid off last week).None of the sources suggested the incident led to Lin’s firing. One Lin defender said he’s never “afraid to talk about how to make a movie better.” Another person familiar with the company said there are any number of filmmakers who could say the same about Lin’s delivery. While it may be juicy to speculate that Gerwig’s follow-up to the game changer “Barbie” could be troubled, don’t forget that the industry doubted that Margot Robbie film right up to opening weekend. “Barbie” grossed $1.44 billion at the worldwide box office and became the highest-earning release in the history of Warner Bros. Pictures.While talk will instantly turn to Lin’s replacement (is it Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy? “Probably,” said one high-placed source), don’t shed too many tears for Lin. He ascended to Netflix from a successful, self-made business in Rideback. “When I took this job, Bela gave me a simple piece of advice: Be yourself,” Lin wrote in a Monday memo obtained by Variety. “You work here because it’s personal. Because of that unspoken pact between your individual passion for movies and the audiences we serve. To them, movies aren’t about business. They’re about feeling something.”

schema.headline: Why Netflix Fired Dan Lin (and the Truth About His Tension With Greta Gerwig Over ‘Narnia’)

title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Sets Oscar Campaigns for Best Picture, Supporting Actress and More Categories
description:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters.

	“You Can See Everything” may rewrite t
body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters.

	“You Can See Everything” may rewrite the rules of the Oscar season.

	Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s A24 documentary, which follows the Theranos founder through the 34 days before she reported to prison and keeps rolling afterward, opened to a staggering $15 million over the weekend, a number most nonfiction films never see in a full run. It’s also boasting a record-setting 99 on Metacritic, 98% on Rotten Tomatoes and holding a 4.7 (out of 5) on Letterboxd and 9.4 on IMDb (as of Monday, Oct. 19). If the IMDb score holds, it will surpass the longstanding No. 1 “The Shawshank Redemption” (1994) as the highest-rated film of all time.
	

	In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture (Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, Tatiana Bears, Maggie Ambrose and Jack Davis), director (Fielder and Oppenheim), production design (Alex DiGerlando and Rebecca Meis), cinematography (David Bolen), costume design (Katina Danabassis), film editing (Adam Locke-Norton), makeup and hairstyling (Stephanie Pasicov and Kerrie Smith), sound (Paul Hsu and Richard Carlos) and original score (Ari Balouzian).


	Variety confirmed exclusively after the film made its surprise world premiere (and general existence became known) at the Telluride Film Festival that Amanda Seyfried, credited in the film as Elizabeth Holmes, is eligible for the Academy Awards in the acting categories. Seyfried, who also appears as herself while reprising her Emmy-winning turn as Holmes from “The Dropout,” will be campaigned in the supporting actress category. If she lands the nomination, it would be her second, following “Mank” (2020). She would get there for playing two people at once: herself and the woman she already won an Emmy statue for playing.
	

	Fielder may also be eligible to submit as a performer, although he is credited as himself. If he was eligible and submitted, the logical home would be lead actor. No actor has ever been nominated for playing themself. The closest we came to seeing this was a person from another A24 film, “Sing Sing” (2023), which had cowriter and star Clarence Maclin vying for consideration in the best supporting actor race, but was ultimately overlooked.

	Christopher Abbott, who also appears in the film as Holmes’ spouse, Billy Evans, in recreated scenes, is also eligible for acting consideration in the supporting actor category.

	Sources close to the awards campaign say the acting push will center on Seyfried regardless.

	No documentary has ever been nominated for best picture in 98 ceremonies. The zeitgeist says this one can be. The awards circuit that usually paves the way is another matter.

	We are in uncharted waters.



	

									Courtesy Everett Collection
	



	Golden Globes: Not eligible based on current written rules, but there could be an avenue.

	The Globes don’t recognize documentaries, which means no picture, no director and no Seyfried. The film cannot be submitted in any category. However, with the acting eligibilities lingering, sources share the group may consider it for this upcoming run. That doesn’t mean it can be eligible across the board. And then in that case, do they consider it a drama or comedy/musical?

	Critics Choice Awards: Eligible across the board, including the acting races.

	That makes Critics Choice the only major stop this season where the performances in “You Can See Everything” could get significant recognition before Oscar nominations.

	Actor Awards: Not eligible but could they make an exception?

	The ceremony formerly known as the SAG Awards does not recognize documentaries, since they aren’t narrative films, even with the narrative recreations woven throughout this one. Seyfried’s path to a supporting actress nomination looked like it would skip the precursor vote by her fellow actors. However, the committee that rules on films is said to be looking at the film to see if it can, in fact, be eligible.

	BAFTA: Still a bit of a question mark but it doesn’t look promising.

	The current rules and guidelines indicate the film can submit in the top categories, but sources say BAFTA may not go for it. Whether Seyfried and Fielder can enter the acting races is less clear. However, indications suggest it may ultimately be eligible for recognition if the voters choose to go for it.
	

	Writers Guild of America: Not eligible.

	The film has no credited screenplay, which isn’t unusual for a documentary but isn’t universal either. Michael Moore’s “Bowling for Columbine” famously won the WGA’s original screenplay prize more than 20 years ago. That won’t be the case here, so “You Can See Everything” won’t be eligible for the Oscars‘ original or adapted screenplay categories.

	Directors Guild of America: Eligible in both top categories.

	This is where it gets interesting. The DGA has a separate documentary category, and its top prize is labeled for directors of a theatrically released feature film. Questions began percolating because of RaMell Ross, whose “Hale County This Morning, This Evening” was nominated for documentary feature at the Oscars before his narrative debut, “Nickel Boys,” was entered in first-time feature director at the DGA, a category he went on to win. 

	This is Fielder’s first directorial credit for a documentary feature, but that isn’t the case for Oppenheim, who helmed “Spermworld” (2024) and “Some Kind of Heaven” (2020). Therefore, the film won’t be eligible for first-time feature director. However, Oppenheim makes his narrative feature directorial debut with the A24 thriller “Primetime” starring Robert Pattinson, Merritt Wever and Skyler Gisondo. He will be vying for one of the five slots in that category. 

	More importantly, under the forward-facing rules, Fielder and Oppenheim are eligible for the DGA’s top award in addition to the documentary prize. That means they could take a slot otherwise slotted for Christopher Nolan (“The Odyssey”) or the other directing duos in the race, including Los Javis (“La Bola Negra”) and Phil Lord and Chris Miller (“Project Hail Mary”).

	ACE Eddies: Eligible

	The guild that represents film editing separates theatrical feature films into four categories: drama, comedy, documentary and animated. Per the rules, “You Can See Everything” would have to choose a category to submit to. A similar situation occurred with Jonas Poher Rasmussen’s animated nonfiction film “Flee” (2021), which was submitted to the guild as a documentary and nominated by ACE Eddie.

	ASC (American Society of Cinematographers): Eligible, but only as a documentary.
	

	Per the rules for the highest award for cinematographers, “All Documentary Feature Films and Documentary Series Episodes must be submitted in the Documentary Award category.”

	Producers Guild of America: Eligible for both the theatrical motion picture award and the documentary prize.

	Add it up and you get a contender with no conventional map. Best picture winners typically announce themselves through the guilds, with a PGA win, a DGA nod, an Actor Awards ensemble slot and a Globe or two along the way. “You Can See Everything” likely won’t be at the Globes. The actors can’t nominate it. BAFTA would be a stop if the rules hold. That leaves the DGA, PGA and Critics Choice as the only places the film can win a top prize and signal whether it’s a historic nominee or something bigger.

	And this raises a bigger question: What if the first documentary nominated for best picture goes all the way to the top prize?

	A few studios are trying to frame the race as David vs. Goliath regarding how they can possibly topple Christopher Nolan’s billion-dollar sensation “The Odyssey.” What if this is actually Odysseus vs. Elizabeth Holmes?

	A caveat that applies to all of the above: every voting body and guild writes its own rules, and any of them can convene a committee to revisit eligibility. So all of these are subject to change. 

	Holmes built a company on the promise that one test could see everything. Awards season has at least six major contests, and as of now, none of them can agree on what they’re actually looking at.

schema.headline: ‘You Can See Everything’ Sets Oscar Campaigns for Best Picture, Supporting Actress and More Categories

title: Tim O’Donnell, Veteran TV Comedy Writer-Director Known for ‘Growing Pains’ and ‘Dave’s World,’ Dies at 77
description: Tim O’Donnell, the veteran comedy writer-director known for his work on sitcoms including “Growing Pains,” “Dave’s World” and “Phil of the Future,”
body:
Tim O’Donnell, the veteran comedy writer-director known for his work on sitcoms including “Growing Pains,” “Dave’s World” and “Phil of the Future,” has died. He was 77.

	O’Donnell died at his home in Glendale, Calif. on July 27. He had struggled with bladder cancer for three years. A memorial service will be held at 2 p.m. on Oct. 25 at the Writers Guild Theater in Beverly Hills.


	O’Donnell was known for his versatility and skill at shaping network TV comedies during the modern heyday of sitcoms. He was also active with the Writers Guild of America West, serving twice on contract negotiating committees and as a board member.
	

	More recently, O’Donnell had worked with Sony Pictures on the studio’s efforts to develop local-language adaptations of sitcoms. He traveled to Russia and China in the 2000s to help instruct local producers on how to craft American-style sitcoms.


	“Tim knew everybody, and he was an astute observer of the business,” said Brian Lowry, a Variety alum and media biz commentator. “As a former news guy, he also recognized the absurdities that populated his new sphere and had the ability not only to laugh at them, but to make others laugh at them as well.”

	O’Donnell grew up in the South Bay area of Los Angeles County and attended Loyola University. His career as a scribe began in local news in Chicago, working for CBS-owned radio and TV stations. He earned local Emmy Awards for his news writing and on-air editorials. He then moved to the West Coast to work for KCBS-TV Los Angeles, where he wrote for the legendary reporter Bill Stout.
	

	O’Donnell eventually moved into narrative TV, serving as a writer, producer and director on such series as ABC’s “Growing Pains” and “Clueless,” CBS’ “Dave’s World” and the short-lived TV adaptation of the 1989 John Candy film “Uncle Buck,” also for CBS. He worked on ABC’s “Home Free,” an early role for Matthew Perry, and Disney Channel’s live-action comedy “Phil of the Future.”  

	O’Donnell was married to Cara O’Donnell for nearly 39 years. His survivors include four children: daughter Kit Michelle O’Donnell Sparke, and three daughters from his first marriage to Vicki Marshall: Shannon O’Donnell Provatas, Carrie O’Donnell VanAckeren and Bridget Morpurgo. He is also survived by four grandchildren.

	The family requests that RSVPs for the Oct. 25 memorial service be sent to jmtsutsui@gmail.com. There will also be a livestream available at this link.

title: Model Sahara Ray Dead at 34
body:
Sahara Ray
                          Model Dead at 34

            Sahara Ray, the Australian model and swimwear designer who once made headlines for her rumored relationship with Justin Bieber, has died ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            "She passed away last night surrounded by family at the hospital. She was so loved," Sahara's family tells TMZ.
      
    
            Her cause of death has not been confirmed.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Ray rose to fame through her modeling career and social media presence, building a massive following on Instagram while launching her own swimwear brand, Sahara Ray Swim.
      

            She made headlines in 2016 when she was photographed vacationing with Bieber in Hawaii. She was also previously romantically linked to Australian singer Cody Simpson.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The model was the daughter of legendary Australian surfer Tony Ray and spent much of her childhood traveling between Australia, California and Hawaii.
      
    
            In 2024, Sahara opened up about her battle with Guillain-Barré syndrome -- a rare neurological disorder that left her partially paralyzed following a serious car accident.
      
    
            She was 34.
      
    
            RIP

            TikToker Dakota Harper says it's all his ex's fault he's been busted for arson ... essentially calling her a bad influence.
      
    
            The social media star -- who's been accused alongside former girlfriend Felicity Eatmon of setting an abandoned home on fire -- told Los Angeles Magazine that he wouldn't be behind bars if he'd just stayed away from her.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In a phone call from a West Virginia Jail, Harper told the outlet ... "I need to stay away from Felicity. She’s the reason I’ve been in jail ... if I stayed away from her, I would not be in any trouble."
      

            He's been in a bit of trouble with the law over the years -- L.A. Mag says he was named in a 2023 truancy complaint for skipping school and was charged in a pending case with misdemeanor unlawful removal, injury to or destruction of property, as well as conspiracy to inflict injury to a person or property this past May.
      
    
            And, as you know, he and Felicity were arrested late last month for allegedly setting a vacant home on fire in Charleston, WV.
      
    
            A judge recently doubled Dakota's bond ... upping it from $10K to $20K.

title: Mariah Carey's Brother's Defamation Lawsuit Dismissed By Judge
description:
Mariah Carey
                          Wins Big Against Brother in Court ... Defamation Suit Dism
body:
Mariah Carey
                          Wins Big Against Brother in Court ... Defamation Suit Dismissed
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              October 19, 2026
                            6:20 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Mariah Carey took home the W in her brother's defamation case against her ... because a judge has ruled in her favor.
      
    
            According to Billboard, a judge dismissed Morgan Carey's case Monday, ruling that he hadn't met the legal requirements to sue his sister.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Here's the deal ... Morgan was trying to sue over Mariah's 2020 memoir, "The Meaning of Mariah Carey," over parts of the book that suggested he'd sold cocaine and been violent during their childhood.
      

            According to Billboard, the judge wrote ... "The Court finds that Plaintiff has not sufficiently pleaded actual malice on the part of Defendant."
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            The judge went on to say Morgan "fails to provide any proof" that Mariah knowingly lied about him in her book.
      
    
            Mariah's attorney, John Rosenberg, told Billboard ... "Ms. Carey is gratified that the Court recognized that her memoir addresses significant issues of public interest and dismissed her brother’s defamation claims in their entirety."
      
    
            Morgan's attorney told the outlet he plans to appeal the dismissal. But until then ... looks like we've got the emancipation of Mimi IRL.

            Mossimo Giannulli doesn't seem to be sweating his divorce from Lori Loughlin ... because he's getting some R&R down in Los Cabos with Hannah Harrison.
      
    
            The 63-year-old fashion designer and the much-younger stylist jetted down to Mexico before the weekend ... a little more than a month after Lori formally filed for divorce.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            While they're a couple of fashionistas, Mossimo and Hannah kept things casual as they touched down south of the border ... he wore jeans and a striped tee, while she rocked baggy pants and a gray zip-up.

title: Atlanta Technical College Student Accidentally Shoots Classmate, Kills Himself
description:
Atlanta Technical College Shooting
                          Man Accidentally Shoots Classmate
body:
Atlanta Technical College Shooting
                          Man Accidentally Shoots Classmate
                          ... Kills Himself
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            A student is dead and another is injured after an accidental shooting at Atlanta Technical College Monday.
      
    
            Atlanta police say one student was carrying a gun that had accidentally discharged inside a classroom, hitting another student in the leg and injuring them.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Investigators say the student with the gun then left the classroom and reportedly went to the bathroom, where he died of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.
      

            The police department's report says an ambulance brought the injured student to the hospital.
      
    
            The report says the injured student was alert, conscious and breathing when officers responded at 8:45 AM, and the college said they are expected to recover.
      
    
            Police say this was an isolated incident and believe there's no active threat to the community. The college says the campus was secured afterward and operations have since resumed.
